lines.text: An island nation with the oldest royal house on Earth, ruled in turn by courtiers, samurai and shoguns. This is the story of Japan, from its first emperors to today.
Tradition says it begins in 660 BCE with Jimmu, the first emperor. Historians date the line much later, but no royal family anywhere has reigned longer.
By about the year 300, the Yamato kings were drawing much of the islands together into one realm, the beginning of the country we know as Japan.
Its people honoured the kami, the spirits of nature, of ancestors and of special places. That faith, Shinto, still fills Japanese life with shrines and festivals.
In 710 the court settled at Nara, a capital laid out on the Chinese model. There the first histories of Japan were written, and a Great Buddha was cast.
In 794 the capital moved again and the Heian period began: four centuries in which life at court became an art in itself.
The new city was Heian-kyo, today's Kyoto. Emperors would live there for more than a thousand years, among temples, shrines and gardens.
At that court lived a noblewoman we know as Murasaki Shikibu. She kept a diary of palace life, and she wrote something far greater.
Her Tale of Genji follows a prince through his loves and sorrows. Written around the year one thousand, it is often called the world's first novel.
But power was slipping from the courtiers to the warriors. In 1185 Minamoto no Yoritomo set up the first shogunate at Kamakura, and the samurai ruled in the emperor's name.
Twice, in 1274 and 1281, Kublai Khan sent great fleets to conquer Japan. Samurai, stone walls and storms drove them back: storms later called kamikaze, the divine winds.
A century on, a shogun built himself a retirement villa in Kyoto, its upper floors covered in gold leaf. It became the Zen temple Kinkaku-ji.
Far to the east stood a small fishing town called Edo. Remember the name: one day it will be Tokyo, one of the largest cities on Earth.
Then the peace broke. From 1467, regional lords fought one another for a century and a half, an age known as the Warring States.
The first to master the chaos was Oda Nobunaga, who put guns to work on a grand scale, until one of his own generals turned on him.
His follower Toyotomi Hideyoshi, a man of humble birth, finished uniting Japan around 1590, and then spent his armies on two failed invasions of Korea.
The third unifier was Tokugawa Ieyasu. He waited for his moment, and then he took everything.
In October 1600, at Sekigahara, his eastern army defeated a western coalition. Three years later he was shogun.
The government he founded, the Tokugawa shogunate, ruled from Edo in the emperor's name for more than two and a half centuries.
This was the Edo period: peace at home, growing towns and busy trade, and strict limits on contact with the outside world.
Himeji Castle dates from these years. Its white plastered walls earned it the name White Heron, and it has come through wars, fires and earthquakes.
In the long peace, the arts flourished. The poet Matsuo Basho walked across Japan and turned the tiny haiku into a great art.
The woodblock artist Katsushika Hokusai filled books with thousands of sketches, and drew Mount Fuji in thirty-six different views.
One of those views shows a huge wave curling over fishing boats, with Fuji small in the distance. The Great Wave became one of the most copied pictures in the world.
In 1852 a prince was born who would give his name to a whole new age: the future Emperor Meiji.
A year later, American warships under Commodore Matthew Perry steamed into Edo Bay and demanded trade. Japan's long isolation was coming to an end.
What followed was a new state, the Empire of Japan. It would industrialise at speed, and take Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria.
It started in 1868 with the Meiji Restoration. The shogun's rule ended, power returned to the emperor, and the army, industry and government were made new.
In 1889 the emperor gave Japan its first modern constitution. It created a parliament, but left great power with the throne, the army and the navy.
That same year in Kyoto, a small company began making playing cards. Its name was Nintendo, and one day it would give the world Mario.
In 1901 Hirohito was born. He would reign from 1926 to 1989, longer than any other emperor in Japanese history.
In 1904 Japan went to war with Russia over Manchuria and Korea, and won. Its victory at sea, at Tsushima, surprised the world.
Akira Kurosawa, born in 1910, would direct Rashomon and Seven Samurai, and bring Japanese cinema to audiences everywhere.
Akio Morita, born in 1921, would help found Sony, and bring out the transistor radio and the Walkman.
In 1923 an earthquake struck Tokyo and Yokohama at midday, as families were cooking. Fire swept the wooden districts, and much of both cities had to be rebuilt.
Osamu Tezuka trained as a doctor, but he drew instead. With Astro Boy and the works that followed, he shaped modern manga and anime.
In 1937 a clash near Beijing grew into a long war with China. It lasted eight years, and millions of Chinese people died.
In 1941 Hayao Miyazaki was born. His hand-drawn fantasies, among them My Neighbor Totoro and Spirited Away, would be loved around the world.
In December 1941, Japanese planes made a surprise attack on the American naval base at Pearl Harbor. The next day the United States was at war.
It ended in August 1945, when atomic bombs fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing about a hundred thousand people at once. Days later, Japan announced its surrender.
Allied forces under Douglas MacArthur occupied the country for seven years. Japan gained a new constitution, land reform and votes for women.
In Tokyo, soon after the war, a small electronics company was founded. It became Sony, maker of the Walkman and the PlayStation.
Shinzo Abe, born in 1954, would serve longer than any other prime minister. In 2022 he was shot dead while giving a campaign speech in Nara.
In 1954, a giant creature woken by nuclear testing rose from the sea to attack Tokyo. Godzilla put the fear of the bomb on screen.
Naruhito, born in 1960, became emperor in 2019 when his father stepped down, the first such abdication in about two hundred years.
And Sanae Takaichi, born in 1961, would become the first woman to be prime minister of Japan, in October 2025.
By 1964 Japan had rebuilt. That year the Shinkansen opened between Tokyo and Osaka, the first high-speed railway of its kind.
Just afterwards, Tokyo hosted the Olympic Games, the first ever held in Asia, and showed the world a modern country.
In the late eighties, prices for land and shares rose to extraordinary heights, and then fell. The slow years that followed are often called the lost decade.
In January 1995 an earthquake struck Kobe. It killed more than six thousand people and brought down an elevated highway, and building rules were changed after it.
In 2011 a huge earthquake and tsunami cut the cooling power at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant. Reactors melted down, and large areas were evacuated.
That earthquake, under the sea off the north-east coast, was the strongest ever recorded in Japan. Its tsunami swept whole towns away.
Tokyo's second Olympic Games were put off for a year by the pandemic, and held in 2021 with almost no spectators.
In 2025 Osaka welcomed the world to an Expo on an artificial island in its bay, built around a great ring of wood.
From divine winds to bullet trains, Japan has remade itself again and again, and its story is still being written.
